options.text: The .xml layout files would be the building's electrical wiring plans (because XML controls component connections), and the .kt files would be the architectural floor plan (because Kotlin defines the overall structure of each room/activity).

The .xml layout files would be the detailed interior design drawings of each individual room — showing what furniture (components) goes where, their sizes, and their visual arrangement. The .kt files would be the operational manual or the contractual rules governing how each room functions — how doors open, what happens when a light switch is flipped, and how rooms connect to each other at runtime.

The .xml layout files and .kt files are both equivalent to different sections of the same blueprint. They are not distinguishable in the analogy because the blueprint represents the entire codebase as one unified document.

The .xml layout files would be the building permit (which must be approved before construction), and the .kt files would be the actual construction materials (bricks, cement). Without approved XML permits, Kotlin construction cannot proceed.

content.explanation: Extending the blueprint analogy: .xml layout files define the visual structure of each screen (like interior design floor plans for each room — what components appear and where). .kt files define the logic and behavior of each screen (like the operational rules — what happens when a button is pressed, how screens navigate to each other). The manifest is the master blueprint tying all rooms together.
hints: XML controls what things look like and where they are positioned.
Kotlin controls what things do — the behavior and logic.
Think of design vs. function.

content.question: A developer has a TextView inside a LinearLayout. They set layout_width='wrap_content' and layout_height='wrap_content'. The text is 'Hello!'. They see the TextView is small and tightly wrapped around the text. Now they copy the entire LinearLayout block (not just the TextView) and paste it to create a second block. The second TextView still says 'Hello!' and is the same size. A colleague says: 'wrap_content makes both TextViews identical in size because they have identical text — this means the size is hardcoded indirectly.' Is the colleague correct? What does wrap_content actually guarantee?

options.text: The colleague is correct. wrap_content for identical text strings always results in exactly the same pixel dimensions. This means wrap_content effectively hardcodes size to match the current text string, and any future text changes will break the layout.

The colleague is incorrect. wrap_content does not hardcode any size. It guarantees that the component will always be exactly as large as its current content requires at render time — no more and no less. If the text of either TextView changes, each one independently resizes to fit its own new content. The two TextViews happen to be the same size right now only because they have the same content, not because wrap_content makes them equal.

The colleague is partially correct. wrap_content hardcodes size to the widest possible text that could be placed in the field — Android pre-calculates the maximum text length for the given font and reserves that space. This prevents layout shifting but does waste some space on shorter strings.

The colleague is correct in effect but wrong in mechanism. wrap_content inherits the size from the first render and caches it permanently. Any text change after the first render requires manually refreshing the layout by calling invalidate() on the view, otherwise the old size persists.

content.explanation: The colleague is wrong. wrap_content does not hardcode any size — it dynamically sizes the component to its content at every render. Both TextViews are currently the same size purely because they contain identical text. If one's text were changed, it would independently resize to fit its new content. This is the exact adaptive nature of wrap_content taught in Episode 3.
hints: wrap_content is dynamic — it adapts at render time.
Size equality for two wrap_content views is coincidental when content is the same.
The moment text changes, the size adjusts independently.

content.question: Across all three Section 5 episodes, the instructor dealt with several situations where a design or code change was made but the result was not yet correct and required iteration. Give the most complete description of all three iterative situations — one from Episode 1, one from Episode 2, and one from Episode 3 — where the instructor tried a value or approach, found it insufficient, and had to adjust to reach the final correct result.

options.text: Episode 1: The EditText width was first set to 274dp (wrong — that is the Button width) and then corrected to 310dp. Episode 2: The exported attribute was first set to 'false' and then corrected to 'true'. Episode 3: The LinearLayout was first set to match_parent and then corrected to wrap_content for its children.

Episode 1: The Button's textSize was first 30dp (too large), then 15dp (not right), and finally settled at 20dp. The ImageView's top margin was first 30dp (not enough), then 80dp, and finally 100dp. Episode 2: The intent-filter was first placed as an attribute inside the opening activity tag (structurally wrong), then correctly moved inside as a child element between opening and closing activity tags. Episode 3: The LinearLayout gave an error without orientation; after adding orientation='vertical', the error was resolved — but then the TextView width was first 100dp (causing overflow and wasted space), leading to the introduction of wrap_content as the correct solution.

Episode 1: The hint attribute on EditText was first set to 'text' (wrong attribute) and then corrected to 'hint'. Episode 2: The Logcat keyword was first searched as 'ERROR' (brought too many results) and then refined to 'FATAL EXCEPTION'. Episode 3: The orientation was first set to 'horizontal' and then corrected to 'vertical' after the layout looked wrong.

Episode 1: The Button was first placed above the password field and then moved below. Episode 2: The manifest file was first opened from the wrong folder and then correctly opened from the manifests folder. Episode 3: The LinearLayout was first placed on the wrong screen (LoginScreen) and then correctly moved to activity_main_two.xml.

content.explanation: Episode 1 had two clear iterative situations: textSize (30dp → 15dp → 20dp) and ImageView margin (30dp → 80dp → 100dp), plus the title TextView margin (20dp → 40dp). Episode 2 had the structural XML iteration where the activity tag had to be changed from self-closing to open/close to accommodate intent-filter as a child element. Episode 3 had the LinearLayout orientation error fix and the demonstration that 100dp fixed width causes problems — which led to the wrap_content lesson.
hints: Look for moments in each episode where the instructor said 'not enough', 'that's too much', or 'let me fix this'.
Episode 1: two or more values were tried before settling.
Episode 3: the 100dp width on TextView directly set up the wrap_content demonstration.
